transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. ____. Um, well, what finally scared me into coming in is that I just keep making these really dumb technical mistakes at work that I absolutely know better than to make. I'm a camera operator and editor, mostly freelance. Which, by the way, the freelance market is so crazy lately. Ever since the strikes, everyone is just scrambling for gigs, and the rates are all over the place. My friend Sarah actually just had to move back to Ohio because she couldn't find enough work, which is wild because she's been out here for like five years and she's so talented. 

But anyway, yeah, I'm making these rookie mistakes. Like, I'll label camera cards wrong, or I'll completely miss a timecode note. And directors can be so picky about timecodes—I worked with this one guy last month who wanted everything logged down to the frame, but he wouldn't even give me a proper script notes file, he just texted me voice memos! Who texts voice memos for edit notes? 

But... right, the mistakes. Like, I'll export a whole client cut with the wrong lower-third graphic on the screen, even after I’ve literally just sat there and checked it. It's just really starting to freak me out.
Were you having this same kind of distractibility and careless mistakes back when you were a child or teenager?

Oh, definitely. Like, even way back in elementary school, my teachers were constantly having to move my desk around. I was just always out of my seat, or I'd be blurting out answers, or bothering my classmates before I even realized I was doing it. 

I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade—she was the one who finally moved my desk right up next to hers. She had this massive collection of ceramic frogs on her desk. Like, an absurd amount of frogs. I think someone gave her one once, and then everyone just assumed she was the "frog lady," so she got them for every holiday. You know how people do that? They latch onto one thing you like and then that's your whole identity for gift-giving. My mom had the exact same thing happen with sunflowers. Our whole kitchen growing up was just covered in sunflower wallpaper, sunflower oven mitts, sunflower plates... I actually can't even look at sunflowers now without feeling a little claustrophobic. I actually shot a wedding last year at a sunflower farm up in Temecula, and the pollen was just an absolute nightmare for my lenses. I spent like three hours cleaning my gear the next day. 

But wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, I was always getting moved because I couldn't just sit still and be quiet.
Have you ever had a period of at least several days when you felt unusually energetic or ‘up’ compared with your normal self?

Um, unusually energetic or 'up'? No, not really. I mean, I'm always kind of on the go, but not like a specific period of being way more up than usual. I'm just consistently... busy. Especially when I'm on set. You have to be, right? You're lugging gear around, running cables, chasing the talent. 

Actually, speaking of running cables, I was on this reality shoot a couple of months ago, and the sound guy—oh my god, this sound guy—he refused to tape down his XLR cables properly. He kept saying it was a "fluid set" and we needed to be mobile. But like, dude, it's a liability! I tripped over his cable right in the middle of a take, almost dropped my RED camera. Do you know how much a RED costs? It's like holding a luxury car in your hands. If I had dropped that, I would have had to sell an organ on the black market to pay for it. Which, honestly, I don't even know how people do that. Like, who is buying black market kidneys? How do you even transport them? Do they just put them in those little Coleman coolers you take to the beach? 

Anyway, sorry. No, I don't think I've ever had a period where I felt, like, unnaturally energetic or anything like that. Just my normal level of bouncing around.
Do these attention and organization problems also happen in your personal life, outside of work?

Um, in my personal life? Well, yeah, I guess so. I mean, I'm definitely not the most organized person at home. My apartment is kind of a disaster zone right now. I have this huge pile of laundry that's been sitting on my chair for, I don't know, a week? Two weeks? It's the chair I'm supposed to use for editing, but I just end up editing on the couch instead because I can't be bothered to move the clothes. 

Which is actually terrible for my back. I bought this ergonomic lumbar pillow from Amazon, but it smells weird. Like... industrial chemicals? I tried airing it out on my balcony, but then my neighbor started complaining about the smell, which is rich coming from him, because he cooks fish in his microwave at like 11 PM. Who microwaves fish? It's a crime against humanity. And the smell just seeps right through the vents into my bathroom. I had to buy all these expensive candles from Anthropologie just to mask it. They have this one that smells like a campfire, which is amazing, but they charge like forty dollars for a piece of wax in a jar. It's a total scam. 

But, uh, yeah, I guess I'm not super organized at home either. It's not just work.
Have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

Depressed or down? Um, no, not really. I mean, I get stressed out, obviously, especially when deadlines are tight or a director is being impossible, but I wouldn't say I've ever felt depressed for two weeks straight. 

I don't even know how people have the time to be depressed for two weeks, honestly. Like, who has that kind of schedule? If I took two weeks off to just feel sad, I'd lose all my clients. Freelance life is brutal that way. You're only as good as your last gig. Like, I did this one music video a few years ago for this indie band—they were trying way too hard to be the next Arctic Monkeys, you know? The lead singer insisted on wearing these vintage leather pants in the middle of July in the desert. We were shooting out in Joshua Tree. It was easily a hundred and ten degrees out there. I kept telling the producer, "Hey, this guy is gonna pass out," and they just brushed me off. And what do you know, three hours in, he completely drops. Face first into a cactus. It was a whole ordeal. We had to call an ambulance, the shoot got shut down, and I still haven't gotten paid for the second half of that day. Which reminds me, I really need to follow up with their management company, but they keep changing their email addresses. It's so shady. 

But yeah, no, I've never had a period where I was just down all day for weeks. Just the usual stress, you know?
